sections.title: What a web developer invoice must show
sections.body: A generic invoice fails when a project scope changes. Your document must clearly separate the agreed project fee from additional hourly work. If you are billing for a specific milestone, name it exactly as it appears in your contract. Include a detailed breakdown of any third-party costs you are passing on, such as software licences or hosting fees. Always attach copies of the original receipts for these expenses. Finally, include your payment terms and state whether the payment is required before the next phase of development begins.
items: Clear distinction between fixed fees and hourly work
Exact milestone names matching your original contract
Itemised third-party costs like hosting and domains
Attached receipts for any passed-through expenses

sections.title: How web developers price and bill their work
sections.body: Most web developers use a hybrid billing model. Large projects usually start with a fixed price, broken into milestones. You might charge a deposit upfront, another payment after the design phase, and a final payment before the site goes live. However, scope creep is inevitable. When a client requests extra pages or complex features, you must bill these as hourly change requests outside the main scope. For ongoing work, developers often sell monthly maintenance retainers to cover security patches, plugin updates, and minor text changes.
items: Fixed prices broken into distinct project milestones
Hourly rates applied to out-of-scope feature requests
Monthly retainers for ongoing maintenance and security patches
Upfront deposits to secure time in your schedule

sections.title: Payment terms, upfront deposits, and chasing late invoices
sections.body: Cash flow is critical for freelance developers. Never start coding without an upfront deposit. A common structure is asking for thirty percent before work begins. To ensure you get paid for the final phase, make it a strict policy to withhold the website launch or the handover of the source code until the final invoice is settled. State this clearly in your terms. If a client ignores a payment request, stop all ongoing development work immediately. Send polite but firm reminders, and do not deploy new features until their account is current.
items: Require an upfront deposit before writing any code
Withhold the final website launch until payment clears
Pause ongoing development if milestone payments are late
State your late payment policies clearly on the invoice

faqs.q: How do I invoice for website hosting and domain names?
faqs.a: List these as separate line items on your invoice. If you are simply passing the cost to the client, include the exact amount and attach the original receipt. If you mark up the hosting for managing the server, label the line item as managed hosting or server administration to explain the higher cost.

faqs.q: Should I charge a deposit before starting a web project?
faqs.a: Yes, you should always charge a deposit. A standard practice is to invoice for twenty-five to fifty percent of the total project cost upfront. This secures the client's commitment and covers your initial time spent on planning, wireframing, and setting up the development environment. Do not begin work until this deposit clears.

faqs.q: How do I handle clients asking for extra features?
faqs.a: When a client asks for work outside the original agreement, inform them immediately that it will cost extra. Create a new line item on your next invoice specifically for out-of-scope change requests. Bill this work at your standard hourly rate, and include a brief description of the new features added.

faqs.q: Can I hold the website launch until the final invoice is paid?
faqs.a: Yes, this is the most effective way to ensure you receive your final payment. State in your initial contract and on your final invoice that the website will not be migrated to the live server until the balance is paid in full. Keep the site on your staging server until the funds clear.
